note: Art direction for Hui Hai (HH1), chosen by the owner on 2026-09-27: the style of the Hàng Trống folk painting 'White Tiger' (Bạch hổ), Hanoi, traditional design (public domain, https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:White_tiger_Hang_Trong.jpg). The Hui Hai are drawn as tiny spirit folk in leaf clothes, never as a picture of the Ba Na people.
style: A painting for a collectible card game, in exactly the art style of the reference image: a Vietnamese Hàng Trống folk painting from old Hanoi: bold, bright, flat colours, a deep cobalt-blue ground, swirling many-coloured cloud scrolls in pink, green, orange and yellow with white outlines, fur, leaves and grass drawn with many fine parallel brush strokes, crisp outlines, a naive, joyful, slightly comic folk charm, flat colour with no realistic shading. Palette: cobalt blue, vermilion, hot pink, leaf green, orange, cream white. IMPORTANT: use ONLY the style of the reference: do NOT draw a tiger or a cat, and do not copy its composition. The subject is a Hui Hai, one of the tiny invisible forest folk of Vietnam's Central Highlands: a thumb-sized spirit person, far smaller than the ferns and pebbles around it, with a round face, big bright eyes and a mischievous little smile, dressed in clothes of woven leaves and fern fronds, a little translucent and shimmering at the edges as if only half there. They are forest spirits, not people: never a picture of any real people or their dress. Gentle, playful, kid-friendly, never scary. One clear main subject, fully in frame. Absolutely no text, letters, Chinese characters, seals, stamps, symbols, logos, borders, card frames or watermarks.

families.Hui Hai: Background: the deep cobalt-blue ground and swirling many-coloured clouds of the reference, over a Highland forest floor of big ferns, bamboo, moss and smooth river pebbles by a clear stream.

heroFamilies.Hui Hai: Background: the deep cobalt-blue ground and swirling many-coloured clouds of the reference, over a Highland forest floor of big ferns, bamboo, moss and smooth river pebbles by a clear stream.

subjects.HH1-H01-kitten: the littlest Hui Hai, the cutest of them all: a tiny girl no taller than a fern leaf, with round cheeks, huge sparkling eyes and a cheeky grin, her hair in a little tuft tied with a grass blade, in a dress of woven green leaves, half-hidden behind a big smooth river pebble that she is lifting with both arms, far too heavy-looking for her size, and she is managing it. A little translucent at the edges, only half there. Not a goddess, no crown, no halo. Playful and captivating.
subjects.HH1-H01-bigcat: the littlest Hui Hai, the cutest of them all: a tiny girl with round cheeks, huge sparkling eyes and a proud grin, in a dress of woven green leaves, now standing on top of a big round boulder in the middle of a clear forest stream, holding a smooth pebble over her head in one hand, easy as anything, while ripples and splashes ring the stream around her and fern fronds bow on both banks. Proud and joyful, still tiny.
subjects.HH1-D01: a Hui Hai of the stream: a tiny spirit boy in a cape of fern fronds, crouched on a wet pebble in a clear, rippling forest stream, grinning as he flicks a little splash of water; around him the ripples are the only sign he is there, and a small fish looks puzzled. Mischievous and cheerful.
subjects.HH1-D02: Yă Hui Hai, Lady of the Ferns: a tiny, wise and kindly Hui Hai grandmother with a serene smile and her white hair in a bun pinned with a thorn, wrapped in a shawl of woven moss and fern, resting at ease curled in the unfurling coil of a giant fern frond, with one small hand on a large rock beside her that she has clearly moved by herself. Calm, strong and gentle.
subjects.HH1-D03: no person: a quiet forest path among ferns and bamboo, and a single smooth round pebble landing with a little bounce and a small puff of dust beside a pair of big muddy human sandals at the edge of the picture; from behind a fern at the side, only the shimmer of a tiny outline and two bright eyes can be seen. Funny and a little mysterious, never scary.
